newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Largest U.S. downstream combine aims at cost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Largest U.S. downstream combine aims at cost.

text.p: Final agreement to merge the Gulf and East Coast U.S. assets of Texaco Inc and Saudi Aramco's Star Refining venture with Royal Dutch/Shell Group will create the second leg of a giant which will have around 13 percent of U.S. refining capacity overall.

The deal puts the last piece of the jigsaw puzzle into place from an earlier agreement between Shell and Texaco to combine on the West Coast and analysts estimate that cost savings across the two ventures could be up to $1.0 billion over three years.
The companies say they have not yet completed an evaluation of possible savings, that they will achieve "substantial savings" without major plant closures.
"Their aim is to cut costs through economies of scale," said Michael Young, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The East/Gulf and West Coast units will be run as two separate companies, but they will have refining capacity of 1.77 million barrels per day and some 26,000 retail outlets.
This refining power, Shell was already the largest in the U.S., puts them way ahead of the rest of the pack where the next biggest players have about a million barrels per day of refining capacity.
The challenge for the U.S. refining industry is to improve return on capital which at six to eight percent is roughly the same as passbook savings.

"There are natural savings where companies have refineries in close proximity, it allows you to combine refineries and the sheer size of Shell and Texaco means you can get large contractual sales of refined products and crude," said Bruce Lanni, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.
The merged group will have huge buying power in crude markets, with 1.77 million barrels per day out of total U.S. capacity of some 14 million barrels.
Auguries of cost savings from other ventures are good.

The European downstream joint venture between British Petroleum Co and Mobil Corp expects $50-$100 million in savings in the second half of this year, while closer to home, Ultramar Diamond Shamrock and Valero Energy Corp have both increased expectations from their recent acquisitions.

Oppenheimer's Lanni notes that the merged company will get a boost from the fact that most refiners have put major capital expenditures behind them and that the refining environment is However, it is not only Shell and Texaco which have had the idea of merging.
"The cost savings opportunities that can be achieved by merging diminish as more and more companies do it," said DMG's Young.
The problem for refiners and gasoline marketers is that competition remains intense and companies are often not able to retain cost savings but have to pass them to the consumer.
The company has to reassure consumer groups and gain approval from the Federal Trade Commission before it starts in 1998.
The companies say they have kept the FTC informed, but consumer groups have also been lobbying hard in Washington.

"I think this is not going to be very different from the impact of the Shell-Texaco merger on the West Coast because both Shell and Star Enterprise are significant marketers and refiners on the East Coast," said Edwin Rothschild, energy policy director for consumer group Citizen Action.
It may also face a legal challenge from other companies, Exxon Corp chairman Lee Raymond said in an magazine interview earlier this year that he was watching the deal closely.
Shell and Texaco say merging is the only way ahead for and industry which has lost 60,000 jobs in the past seven years. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
